prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

1 I find a strange knowledge of wind, an open door in the mountain pass where everything intersects. Believe me. This will not pass. This is a world where flags contain themselves, and are still, marked by their unfurled edges. Lean stuff sways on the boughs of pitch pine: silver, almost tinsel, all light gone blue and sprouting orange oils in a last bouquet. 2 These were the nest builders; I caught one last morning, I sang so it fell down, stupid, from the trees. They’re so incorrect in their dead skin. Witness their twig feet, the mistake of their hands. They will follow you. They yearn pebbles for their gullets to grind their own seed. They swallow so selflessly and die like patriots. 3 Last Christmas, a family of five woke from their dreaming and dreamed themselves over: the baby in its pink pajamas, the boy in the red flannel bathrobe he grabbed from the door, a mother, a father, and a sister in curlers; all died. A wood frame house, a cannister of oil, a match—watch as it unsettles. They were so cold; umber. 4 I am away from the knowledge of animal mystics, brujas and sorcerers or the nudging chants of a Tlingit Kachina. I am frightened by regions with wills of their own, but when my people die in the snow I wonder did the depths billow up to reach them?

Keywords: Believe, This, Lean

outputs.L1:
1. I find a strange knowledge of wind: an open door in the mountain pass where everything intersects. Believe me—this will not pass. This is a world where flags contain themselves and remain still, marked by their unfurled edges. Lean things sway on the boughs of pitch pine: silver, almost tinsel, all light turned blue and sprouting orange oils in a final bouquet.

2. These were the nest builders. I caught one last morning; I sang, and it fell, stupid, from the trees. They are so incorrect in their dead skin. Witness their twig feet, the error of their hands. They will follow you. They yearn for pebbles in their gullets to grind their own seed. They swallow so selflessly and die like patriots.

3. Last Christmas, a family of five woke from their dreaming and dreamed themselves over: the baby in pink pajamas, the boy in the red flannel bathrobe he grabbed from the door, a mother, a father, and a sister in curlers—all dead. A wood-frame house, a canister of oil, a match: watch as it unsettles. They were so cold; umber.

4. I am far from the knowledge of animal mystics, brujas and sorcerers, or the nudging chants of a Tlingit Kachina. I am frightened by regions with wills of their own; but when my people die in the snow, I wonder: did the depths billow up to reach them?
outputs.L2:
1. I come upon an uncanny understanding of the wind, a gap like an entrance cut through the mountain pass, a place where all things meet. Trust me: this is not going away. Here, flags seem to fold their own meaning inside themselves, motionless, defined only by the borders that once spread outward. Thin things tremble on the pitch-pine branches—silver, nearly like tinsel, with the light turned blue and orange oils budding out in one final bouquet.

2. These were the ones that made nests. Yesterday morning I caught one; I sang, and it dropped foolishly out of the trees. Their dead skin looks so wrong. Look at their little twig-like feet, the error of their hands. They will trail after you. They long for stones in their throats, pebbles to help grind the seeds they eat. They take everything in with such self-sacrifice, and they perish like loyal citizens.

3. Last Christmas, five members of one family woke out of sleep and entered another dream entirely: the baby wearing pink pajamas, the boy in the red flannel robe he snatched from the door, the mother, the father, and a sister with curlers in her hair. Every one of them died. A wooden house, a container of oil, a single match—see how quickly it all becomes unstable. They had been terribly cold; brown as umber.

4. I stand apart from the lore of animal mystics, from brujas and sorcerers, from the quiet urging of a Tlingit Kachina’s chants. Places that seem to possess intentions of their own terrify me. Yet when my people die out in the snow, I ask myself whether the deep places rose and swelled upward to meet them.
outputs.L3:
The speaker describes a mysterious mountain pass where wind, light, and the surrounding natural elements seem to gather in a strange and uneasy balance. It is not simply a place of beauty, but one of unsettling stillness, as though the landscape is holding its breath. The wind moves through the pass with a force that feels almost deliberate, while the light shifts across stone, snow, and open air in ways that make the place seem both alive and indifferent. Everything there appears suspended between motion and silence, creating the impression that something unseen is present.

From this landscape, the speaker turns inward and reflects on birds, or perhaps all nest-building creatures, as fragile and imperfect beings. They are driven by instinct to create shelter, to protect their young, and to endure hardship, yet their efforts are always vulnerable to failure. Their nests are temporary, their bodies delicate, and their sacrifices often go unnoticed. In this reflection, the speaker sees a kind of tragic nobility: these creatures continue building and caring despite their weakness, guided by impulses they may not understand but cannot resist.

The memory of a family of five who died in a winter house fire deepens this sense of vulnerability. The speaker remembers them not as distant figures, but as human beings caught in a moment of absolute helplessness. The cold surrounding the event is emphasized, making their deaths feel even more stark and sorrowful. Fire, which should bring warmth, becomes the cause of destruction, while winter waits outside with its own deadly force. The image of the family dying in such conditions suggests how thin the barrier is between shelter and danger, life and exposure.

Although the speaker resists mystical or supernatural explanations, they cannot fully dismiss the fear that certain landscapes seem to possess a will of their own. The speaker does not want to believe in spirits, omens, or conscious forces hidden in the mountains and snow, yet the feeling remains. Some places appear too powerful, too charged with silence and weather, to be understood as merely passive. The speaker is unsettled by the possibility that the natural world, though not mystical in any simple sense, may still act with a force that feels intentional.

In the end, the speaker wonders whether nature itself somehow rose up to claim the people who died in the snow. This thought is not offered as a clear belief, but as a troubling question. The deaths of the family, the cold, the fire, the wind, and the mountain pass all merge into a single atmosphere of dread. The speaker is left contemplating whether human beings are ever truly separate from the landscapes around them, or whether, in moments of disaster, the natural world reveals its power to take back what is fragile, warm, and briefly alive.
outputs.L4:
The piece presents death not as a distant abstraction but as an uncanny force moving through a severe, living landscape. The natural world is harsh and animated: winter is not merely a season, the cold is not merely weather, and the surrounding terrain seems to possess a strange awareness of human suffering. Through fragmented, lyrical images, the text creates an atmosphere in which reality feels broken apart by grief. Birds appear as symbolic figures, suggesting omens, spirits, witnesses, or messengers between the living and the dead.

At the center of the text is the remembered catastrophe of a family burning in winter. This memory gives the landscape its emotional and spiritual weight. Fire and snow, warmth and freezing, life and death are brought into violent contact, making the disaster feel both physically vivid and almost mythic. The event is not explained in ordinary terms; instead, it lingers as a wound in memory, surrounded by images that make it seem larger than a single human tragedy.

The text suggests that nature and disaster may possess a kind of will, or at least that grief makes them feel that way. The world appears charged with intention, as if birds, weather, fire, and darkness are participating in the loss. This creates a mystical or uncanny mood, where the boundaries between accident, fate, and supernatural presence blur. Human death becomes terrifyingly intimate because it is tied to family, memory, and the body, yet it also feels beyond rational understanding. The result is a haunting meditation on loss, in which the landscape seems to remember the dead and death itself becomes part of the living world.

Believe this: every great change begins with a small decision. It may not look powerful at first, and it may not feel certain, but the moment you choose to keep going, you create momentum.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem in four numbered sections, using wintry mountain imagery, birds, folklore, and a tragic house fire, in a dense lyrical style.
counterfactuals.output:
1.

Above the village the mountains wore winter like a crown of drowned bells, each peak bluing into the next until the sky seemed stitched from old milk and raven-feathers. Snow fell upward there, or so the grandmothers said, lifting the footprints of the dead back into the clouds. At dusk the pines bent their black antlers and listened for the fox-bride combing frost from her hair. Birds gathered in the weather: bullfinches with coals in their throats, crows with inked subpoenas, owls pale as unsent letters. They circled the chimney-smoke and read in it the gossip of the buried springs, the names of children not yet born, the small gray future shivering under every door.

2.

Our house stood at the foot of the pass, nailed together from storm-light and grandfather’s curses, with a roof that groaned beneath the snow like an animal remembering the trap. In the pantry, onions sprouted green horns; in the attic, sleigh bells rusted in a chest beside a bridal veil bitten by mice. Mother kept the old tales folded under her tongue: of the witch who warmed her hands inside a wolf, of the saint who turned into a hawk to escape his own prayers, of the mountain king sleeping beneath the glacier with a candle for a heart. Each night the lamp flame bowed to these stories, thin and yellow, while outside the wind dragged its invisible cart through the drifts, heaped high with bones of travelers and the feathers of impossible birds.

3.

The fire began like a secret learning to speak. First a red syllable under the stove, then a sentence along the wall, then the whole house reciting its destruction in a language of resin and wool. Windows burst into stars. The roof lifted one black wing and fell. Snow came down, astonished, unable to save what it loved; it hissed on the beams, turned to tears, vanished. Father ran back for the cradle, or the icon, or the cat—no one agrees, and the dead are poor witnesses. Above us, birds erupted from the orchard, sparrows and crows and one white owl, all flung upward as if the house had been their burning nest. Their cries braided with ours until grief had a weather of its own.

4.

In spring, though spring was only winter with green eyes, we found among the ashes a melted spoon, three nails, the cracked blue bead from Mother’s rosary, and a print in the soot shaped like a bird’s foot or a child’s hand. The villagers said the mountain had taken payment; the grandmothers said the fox-bride had passed too near; the priest said nothing, only scattered salt where the door had been. At night I dream the house still stands, lit from within by gentle flames, and my family moves room to room as bright as saints behind glass. Snow taps the window with its many fingers. A crow in the chimney whispers my name, then my name backward, and somewhere high above the pass the frozen peaks open their mouths and sing smoke into the stars.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an experimental literary passage that sounds like contemporary avant-garde poetry: fragmented, ominous, numbered 1–4, with themes of wind, pine trees, dead birds, Christmas, and Indigenous mysticism.
counterfactuals.output:
1.  
Wind worries the house-bones.  
Pine trees lean in, black-green witnesses,  
needles clicking like teeth in a jar.  

On the porch: a dead bird,  
small fist of weather,  
its eye holding the last gray inch of sky.  

Christmas lights blink  
as if sending distress  
to a god with no address.  

2.  
Snow begins, then stops, ashamed.  
The road is a long animal  
pretending to sleep.  

Somewhere beyond the pines,  
a drumbeat—or a branch knocking—  
or the old world asking not to be named.  

I do not touch what is sacred.  
I stand outside it,  
cold in my borrowed language.  

3.  
Dead birds in the ditch.  
Dead birds beneath the mailbox.  
Dead birds arranged by no hand  
into a grammar of warning.  

The wind reads them aloud.  
The pines refuse translation.  

Inside, a plastic angel  
glows above the television,  
blue-faced, electric,  
terrible with mercy.  

4.  
Christmas morning:  
ash in the snow,  
feathers in the sink,  
sap on the doorframe.  

The wind comes dressed as a relative.  
It knows every name we buried.  

Pines bow, not to us.  
Something ancient moves past the window—  
not spectacle, not story,  
only presence,  
only dark breathing through the needles.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dark, poetic vignette sequence about nature, death, and superstition, mixing precise sensory description with unsettling dream logic.
counterfactuals.output:
I.

At dusk the reeds begin counting.

Not aloud, not in any tongue a living mouth can answer, but by the dry clicking of their stems as the wind passes through them—one, one, one, each reed alone in its arithmetic. The marsh has no shore tonight. It only thickens outward, black water shouldering under the grass, a slow animal breathing mud.

A heron stands in the shallows with the patience of a widow.

Its eye is a pinprick of old brass. Its legs vanish beneath water filmed with pollen and drowned gnats. When it moves, it does so as if remembering a murder. The fish below do not scatter. They rise belly-up in small pale moons, and the heron bends to take them from the surface as though accepting coins from the dead.

Beyond the reeds, someone has hung red thread from the alder branches.

It twists there, wet and trembling.

No one admits to tying it.

Everyone knows what it means.

II.

The orchard was planted over a plague pit, though the family denies this at supper.

Still, every autumn the apples bruise from the inside first. Bite one and the flesh is cold as cellar stone, sweet with rot, marked by a brown star where the teeth meet. Children are told not to swallow the seeds. Children swallow them anyway and dream of roots growing through their ribs, of white blossoms opening from their mouths while their mothers weep and prune them.

Tonight the trees are full of birds that should have flown south weeks ago.

They sit in the branches like charred fruit.

No wind moves them. No wing stirs. Now and then one drops to the ground with a sound like a fist in flour. In the morning, the old women will turn each corpse over with a spoon and search its breast for signs: a clot shaped like a cradle, a worm knotted into a letter, the tiny black nail of a saint.

If the nail points east, there will be a birth.

If it points west, the well must be covered.

If it points nowhere, no one speaks until noon.

III.

In the house by the quarry, the mirrors are veiled whenever thunder comes.

Not for lightning. Not for fear of broken glass.

For the thing that leans close from the other side when the air turns green.

The grandmother knows its face. She saw it once as a girl, reflected in a spoon while her father lay dying upstairs. It had antlers still velveted with blood and the soft, worried eyes of a calf. It opened its mouth against the silver bowl of the spoon, and from it came the smell of wet wool, extinguished candles, and freshly cut yew.

Her father died before dawn.

Since then, whenever thunder drags its iron cart over the hills, she pins black cloth over every mirror and turns the spoons face down.

But tonight she forgets one.

A little hand mirror, cracked at the edge, lies beneath a pillow in the spare room where no guest has slept for seven years. At midnight the storm lowers itself onto the roof. Rain fills the gutters with frantic fingers. The quarry flashes white.

In the hidden mirror, something begins to chew its way through the dark.

IV.

The fox comes three nights after the burial.

It sits on the grave mound, neat as a flame, its paws black with churchyard soil. The moon lays a blade along its back. It watches the kitchen window where the widow stands holding a cup of milk gone blue in the cold.

She knows better than to call it by her husband’s name.

She knows better than to look away first.

The fox opens its mouth. No bark comes. Instead, the widow hears the clink of his wedding ring in the washbasin, the cough he hid behind his hand, the low whistle he made when sharpening knives. She hears him turning in bed beside her, though the bed upstairs is flat and white and empty. She hears him saying the small, ordinary cruel things that only the beloved are permitted to say.

The cup cracks between her hands.

Milk spills over her wrists.

By morning there are fox tracks in the ashes of the hearth, circling the cold grate seven times.

V.

Deep in the fir wood, mushrooms gather where the deer die.

They come overnight: slick caps the color of liver, pale stems translucent as grubs, gills fine and pink as infant lungs. They push through the moss around the carcass in a ring so perfect it seems measured by a careful god. The deer lies at the center, folded awkwardly, its eyes taken, its tongue blackening between its teeth.

The villagers never step inside such rings.

They leave pins, bread crusts, drops of blood from the thumb.

They say the little people dance there.

They say many things to avoid saying hunger.

This morning a girl in a blue coat finds the ring and crouches at its edge. Her breath smokes. Her stomach snarls. She has been told the rules, but rules are thinner than winter.

She reaches in.

The mushrooms feel warm.

When she pulls one free, the deer lifts its head and looks at her with the face of her unborn child.

VI.

There is a pond beyond the last pasture where the dead leaves never sink.

They float all year, even under ice: oak, beech, ash, rowan, each one black-veined and glossy, turning slowly on water so clear it seems absent. In summer, dragonflies stitch blue fire over the surface. In winter, the ice seals them beneath like messages pressed under glass.

No one drinks from the pond.

The cattle refuse it. Dogs whine and crawl on their bellies when brought near. A priest once blessed it and lost his voice before reaching the road. For the rest of his life he spoke only in the cries of birds: rook at funerals, lark at baptisms, owl in the hour before death.

At the bottom of the pond is a door.

At least, that is what the children say.

A green door with a brass handle, standing upright in the silt, where no wall is and no house was ever built. On certain nights, when fog lies low and the moon is no more than a blind eye behind cloud, the handle turns.

Then every leaf on the surface turns with it.

VII.

The hare is bad luck only when it crosses from right to left.

Left to right means rain. Straight toward you means a letter. Away from you means someone has lied.

But a hare standing upright in a field of frost means nothing good has a name.

At dawn the farmer sees it among the turnips, balanced on its hind legs like a little gray man. Its ears are long and black-tipped. Its chest flutters. Frost has silvered each whisker. Around it, the field is full of footprints: hare tracks, child tracks, hoofprints, bare human feet, all circling, circling, never entering the place where the animal stands.

The farmer spits over his shoulder.

The hare spits back.

Its saliva steams on the frozen leaves. Where it falls, the turnips split open, revealing not white flesh but rows of tiny teeth.

VIII.

When the old oak finally falls, it does not fall downward.

It falls into yesterday.

One moment it stands at the edge of the lane, hollow and vast, its dead limbs lifted like a warning. The next, there is only a stump wet with sap and a tremor in the air, as if a giant door has closed behind it.

The villagers remember shade where none remains. They remember carving initials into bark that is no longer there. They remember hanging a murderer from the lowest branch, though no record names him. They remember courting beneath its leaves, hiding from rain, finding a child asleep among its roots with a moth on her tongue.

By evening, acorns begin raining from the empty air.

They strike roofs, skulls, water troughs. They bounce down chimneys and roll beneath beds. Crack one open and it is full of black hair. Crack another and a beetle crawls out wearing the face of a bride.

The oldest man in the village gathers three acorns in his cap and carries them to the crossroads.

He buries them there before moonrise.

“Best not to let memory seed,” he says.

But all night long, something under the road pushes upward.

IX.

In the cemetery, snow falls only on the unvisited graves.

It comes lightly at first, a powdering over names softened by lichen, over angels with broken noses, over lambs carved for children who would be older than grandmothers now. The tended graves remain bare. Their flowers blacken in the frost. Their candles gutter in red glass. But on the forgotten dead, the snow gathers thick and blue.

By January, those graves resemble sleeping animals.

By February, they breathe.

The caretaker hears them while sharpening his spade in the shed: a long, muffled exhalation from beneath the drifts. He tells himself it is thaw. He tells himself it is foxes tunneling. He tells himself many sensible lies and hangs horseshoes over both doors.

On the first Sunday of March, a woman comes searching for a grave with no stone.

She carries no flowers, only a bowl of salt.

“Where is he?” she asks.

The caretaker points to the deepest mound.

She kneels, pours the salt in a circle, and presses her ear to the snow.

Underneath, someone knocks three times.

X.

Before spring, the river gives back what it has taken.

Not all of it. Never all.

A boot with the foot still inside. A cradle gone soft with weeds. A sack of kittens, each with a pearl of ice in its mouth. Once, a whole bell from the drowned chapel upstream, green with slime and silent until a boy touched it; then it rang beneath his palm, and every woman in the village began to cry milk.

This year the river returns a man made of roots.

He washes up in the reeds at first light, tangled in his own wooden fingers. His skin is bark. His beard is moss. Minnows flicker in the hollows of his chest. Where his eyes should be, two hazelnuts gleam, smooth and watchful.

The men fetch ropes. The women make signs against envy, drowning, and sudden love.

When they drag him onto the bank, he leaves behind a dark imprint in the mud shaped exactly like a cradle.

No one speaks.

The root-man opens one splintered hand.

Inside lies a fresh green leaf, folded like a tongue.

XI.

At last the thaw comes, and with it the flies.

They wake in window frames, in church corners, in the seams of old coats. They crawl from the mouths of dead mice and the eyes of saints painted on wood. They gather on the first lamb born wrong, the one with two faces, both bleating. They polish themselves in the sunlight as if preparing for a feast.

The village smells of wet earth, manure, smoke, and something sweeter underneath.

Something opening.

In the woods, bluebells spread like spilled dusk. In the ditches, frogspawn clouds the water. Lambs stagger on new legs. Worms rise blind from the soil. The world puts on green with the indifference of a corpse being dressed.

Every door has a charm nailed above it: rowan twig, iron nail, hare bone, red thread.

Every charm casts a shadow shaped like a hand.

At night, the people dream the same dream.

They dream they are lying beneath the fields, listening to roots drink from their hearts. Above them, the grass grows bright and terrible. Above that, the hares dance upright. Above that, the moon lowers itself like a white face to the earth and whispers the name each person will have after death.

No one remembers the names upon waking.

But all morning, they taste soil on their tongues.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: I want a haunting prose poem with numbered paragraphs, first-person narration, strange animal imagery, references to brujas/sorcerers/Tlingit spirits, and an ending about people dying in the snow.
counterfactuals.output:
1. I was born under a porch where the dogs would not sleep, between a jar of black salt and a nest of blind mice. My mother said the brujas had passed over the house that night, their skirts stitched with beetle wings, their mouths full of rainwater. I remember the moon looking down like a skinned rabbit.

2. Since then, animals have followed me badly. A deer with a child’s hands. A rooster that crowed from the bottom of a well. Moths the size of hymnals beating themselves to powder against my windows. Once, in the market, a fish opened its silver mouth and called me by my dead name.

3. The sorcerers came later, men with tobacco-colored fingers and eyes like wet stones. They did not ask for money. They asked for my shadow. They said it had been walking ahead of me, frightening horses, kissing mirrors, lying down in graves that were not yet dug. I told them I needed it. They laughed softly, as if I had claimed to own the wind.

4. In the north, where the mountains sharpen themselves on the sky, I heard stories of Tlingit spirits moving through cedar smoke and raven-dark water. I did not speak their names lightly. I only listened as the old trees creaked like doors in a house no human had built, and something with antlers of ice stepped between the trunks without breaking a twig.

5. I have carried these visitations inside me like eggs. Some nights they hatch. A fox with a woman’s braid crawls from my throat. A black dog sleeps in my ribcage and dreams of fire. My hands smell of feathers though I have touched nothing living. I wake to find hoofprints circling my bed, each one filled with milk.

6. There are towns I cannot return to. In one, the church bells rang underwater for three days. In another, every mirror showed a room behind me where brujas combed their hair with fishbones and waited for me to turn around. I kept walking. I always keep walking. That is the spell I was given: never arrive, never be forgiven.

7. Winter found me at last in a country of white fields and black pines. The sky lowered itself like a coffin lid. I saw the sorcerers again, far off, or perhaps only crows standing upright in the storm. I called to them, but the snow took my voice and folded it away.

8. By morning, the road was gone. The houses were gone. Even the wolves had become thoughts of wolves. I lay down where the drifts were deepest and listened to the world filling in its own footprints. All around me, people were dying in the snow, quietly, one by one, as if returning to a language the cold had been speaking forever.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a cryptic winter-themed piece of literary fiction in the voice of a disturbed observer, including flags, pitch pine, nest-building birds, a family killed by fire, and fear of landscapes that seem alive.
counterfactuals.output:
At the first snow I began to see the fields breathing.

No one believed me, because no one looked long enough. They hurried from their cars to the post office, from the church steps to the butcher’s awning, their collars raised, their faces shut like cupboards. But I watched. I had always watched. The hill beyond the depot lifted itself in the blue hour and lowered again under the skin of frost, and the black ditches along the road opened and closed like mouths rehearsing my name.

All winter the flags snapped themselves to threads.

They hung from porches and school roofs and the little cemetery where the veterans lay in rows, red and white and blue beaten pale by weather, each flag a tongue that could not stop warning us. I counted them daily. Twenty-seven in town, nine on the road to the mill, three at the burned place if you counted the one melted into the gutter and the two that children had planted in the snow for reasons no one explained.

The burned place had been a farmhouse before the fire took it—white clapboards, green shutters, a pitch pine leaning over the well with its needles full of crows. A family lived there: father, mother, two girls, one boy small enough to still mispronounce chimney. They died in their beds, they said, though beds were only iron after, and the house only a black fist.

People called it an accident. People love a word that locks the door.

I had seen the smoke that night. I had seen it rise straight up though there was wind. I had seen sparks moving against the sky like insects returning to a hive. And in the morning, when the men gathered with hooks and shovels, I saw the pitch pine standing unburned, resin shining in the cold, every needle intact. At its base the snow had melted in a perfect circle.

Birds came there after.

This was wrong. In deep winter no bird should concern itself with nests, not in our country, where the ponds go iron-hard and the foxes scream under the moon. Yet there they were: jays, sparrows, two blackbirds glossy as wet coal, tugging fibers from the ruined curtains, lifting hair from the ash, threading straw through the ribs of the house. They built in the pitch pine, not one nest but many, cramped together like thoughts in a sick mind.

I tried to tell Mr. Vale at the store.

“Birds build in spring,” he said, weighing potatoes.

“These do not know it is winter.”

“Then they’re fools.”

“No,” I said. “They’ve been told something.”

He put one extra potato in the sack and would not meet my eye.

By January, the snow had covered the foundations. Only the chimney remained, black and upright, a finger pressed to the lips. The flags at the road froze in their own gestures. The birds worked in silence. The pine bent lower each week, though no storm touched it, until its branches seemed to be listening at the buried windows.

I stopped sleeping. Whenever I closed my eyes, I saw the landscape turn its head.

The pond watched me first. Then the quarry. Then the ridge behind the school, that long white animal with spruce along its spine. I felt their attention gathering. I felt the town held in the cup of something patient and ancient, something that had worn barns and churches the way a man wears gloves.

One evening I walked to the burned place with a lantern and a hatchet. The snow squealed under my boots. No smoke rose, no bird called, but the nests shifted as I approached, all of them packed into the pine like dark fruit.

I stood beneath the branches and smelled not ash, not sap, but warm bread.

From inside the chimney came the sound of children turning in sleep.

I dropped the hatchet. The pine shivered. The flags along the road began all at once to strain toward me, stiff with frost, pointing, pointing. The hill behind the house swelled under its white blanket, and the fields inhaled so deeply that the snow cracked from fence to fence.

Then I understood: the family had not burned.

They had been taken indoors by the winter.

And the birds, mad little carpenters, were building them a way back.
